paragraphs.text: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric and medical condition once described as the “relentless pursuit of thinness” [1]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Disorders, fifth edition (DSM-5), was pub lished in 2013 and includes a significantly revised eating disorder section. By the new cri teria, recent prevalence data estimate the rate of AN to be 4% among females and 0.3% among males, with a stable overall incidence rate over the past several decades, but increased incidence among youth <15 years [2]. The disorder is most commonly seen among adolescent girls (i.e., assigned female at birth) of postindustrialized, high-income countries, with estimates that 19–30% of younger patients with AN are male, and the overall prevalence of this disorder among adolescent boys appears to be increasing [3, 4]. Testosterone deficiency and many endo crine alterations seen in girls are also seen in adolescent boys with this diagnosis [5, 6]. The overall prevalence of AN has also risen dra matically since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with both inpatient and outpatient programs seeing a 3–4-fold increase in the prevalence of all restrictive eating disorders compared to prepandemic rates [7]. Another newly identified risk group are lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender youth who fre quently exhibit body image distortion and dis ordered eating [8]. Eighty-five percent of patients with AN present between the ages of 13 and 20 years during a critical period for growth, pubertal development, and maximal bone accretion that culminates in peak bone mass. The disorder can result in a compromise in each of these important endocrinologic events, with lifelong sequelae. Reports over the past decade document an earlier age of onset of AN [9], and it is recognized that onset at a younger age is associated with less opti mal growth and bone health outcomes [10].
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Patients with AN also have a characteristic clinical picture of endocrine dysfunction, including amenorrhea, abnormal temperature regulation, elevated growth hormone (GH) levels associated with lower levels of insulin like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), hypercorti solemia, and abnormal eating suggestive of hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction [11]. Therefore, endocrine function has been stud ied extensively in these patients. The multiple endocrine abnormalities appear to represent an adaptation to the starvation state.
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The clinical features of AN by DSM-5 criteria are shown as follows. Amenorrhea was excluded as a diagnostic criteria with the DSM-5 publication in 2013 [12]. However, the absence of amenorrhea among the diagnostic criteria should not diminish bone health con cerns in the young woman who manifests all other features. There can still be hormonal alterations at play that pose a risk to bone health despite ongoing menses. Furthermore, despite amenorrhea no longer being required for the diagnosis of AN, a larger proportion of patients with this condition are, in fact, amenorrheic.

paragraphs.text: requirements, leading to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health. Significantly low weight is defined as a weight that is less than minimally normal or, for children and adolescents, less than that minimally expected. 2. Intense fear of gaining weight or of

paragraphs.text: becoming fat or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight. 3. Disturbance in the way in which one’s
body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

Patients with AN exhibit hyperactivity of their hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis [13–15]. These patients typically have ele vated serum cortisol concentrations, accom panied by increased corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) secretion and normal circu lating levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The elevation in cortisol appears to be secondary to increased cortisol produc
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal Axis in AN

paragraphs.text: tion, decreased clearance, or a combination of both factors [14]. Boyar and colleagues [16] were the first to report decreased cortisol metabolism in AN, subsequently confirmed by other groups. Walsh and colleagues [17] noted that when body size was taken into account (cortisol production/kg), cortisol secretion was significantly increased.
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal Axis in AN

paragraphs.text: Overactivity of the HPA axis is largely sec ondary to increased CRH production but with circadian rhythmicity maintained. Adolescents with AN, as compared to healthy controls, have higher cortisol due to increased frequency of secretory bursts, suggesting increased cortisol secretion in this population [18]. Patients with AN may also exhibit inad equate suppression of cortisol after an over night oral dexamethasone challenge [17, 19]. Estour and colleagues [20] administered dexa methasone intravenously to 15 patients with AN and observed nonsuppression in 93%. Results of those studies suggest that the hypercortisolism seen in AN is not suppress ible by exogenous glucocorticoid. The abnor malities appear to improve after refeeding and weight gain. Gold and colleagues [13] found increased cortisol response to CRH, while Hotta and colleagues [21] showed a decreased response. Both the groups interpret their find ings as an indication that there is increased HPA axis activity due to increased CRH secretion in AN. Higher cortisol levels in AN contribute to both reproductive dysfunction and low bone density.
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal Axis in AN

paragraphs.text: The adrenal androgens dehydroepiandros terone (DHEA) and DHEA sulfate (DHEAS) have been reported to be abnormal in some, although not all, studies in young women with AN. In adult women with AN, DHEAS has been shown to be decreased [22, 23], increased [24], or unchanged [25, 26] as compared to healthy controls. In adolescents with AN, DHEAS inversely correlates with markers of bone resorption [27]. A combination regimen of oral DHEA, estrogen, and progestin was found to be safe and effective for preserving BMD in young women with AN [28]. A fol low-up study showed significant changes in measures of hip strength and cross-sectional geometry in the treated group compared to
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal Axis in AN

paragraphs.text: placebo that may translate to a lower fracture risk [27, 29]. Of concern, however, a subse quent clinical trial did not show the skeletal benefit of combined adrenal/gonadal hormone replacement that was seen in earlier studies of older adolescents and young women; in fact, a deleterious effect was observed in those with open epiphyses [30]. Thus, there appears to be a differential effect in efficacy among adolescents with open vs. closed epiphyses, limiting the applicability of this therapeutic option for adolescents.
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal Axis in AN

paragraphs.text: Studies examining the question of insulin dynamics in AN have yielded contradictory results [31], demonstrating both insulin resis tance and insulin deficiency in these patients. Low fasting glucose and insulin concentra tions have been reported in AN [27], as have both normal [32] and increased insulin sensi tivity [33]. Patients with AN have also demon strated subnormal insulin rises after oral dexamethasone compared to healthy, normalweight controls [34]. Thus, adolescents with AN exhibit either an isolated resistance to glucocorticoids at a pancreatic level or com promised pancreatic function after months of starvation, with a diminished ability to respond to high-glucose challenge.
paragraphs.heading: in AN

paragraphs.text: Leptin, a peptide hormone secreted by adipose tissue (e.g., adipokine) that is osteo anabolic, is altered by adaptations to a starva tion state [35]. The subnormal plasma leptin concentrations seen in AN [36] likely reflect the decreased fat mass in these subjects. Subnormal leptin levels in patients with amen orrhea suggest that this hormone may serve as a metabolic signal to the reproductive axis [37–39]. Mantzoros and colleagues supported this theory through a study of eight women with hypothalamic amenorrhea, demonstrat ing that leptin administration improved repro ductive, thyroid, and growth hormone axes and increased markers of bone formation
paragraphs.heading: in AN

paragraphs.text: [38]. However, patients receiving leptin replacement had a decrease in weight and fat mass in two trials [40, 41], raising concerns regarding its clinical utility. Nonetheless, there remains interest in the potential use of leptin for young women with AN, and additional clinical trials are necessary [42].
paragraphs.heading: in AN

paragraphs.text: Adiponectin, another adipokine produced by adipocytes, varies inversely with fat mass [43]. Low levels of adiponectin are associated with insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia [43]. Adiponectin has been shown to be both elevated [43] and low [44] in adult women with AN. Similarly, adiponectin levels have been reported as normal [45] or elevated [46, 47] in adolescents with AN, as compared to healthy controls and may explain in part the variabil ity of BMD seen in these patients [45]. Alterations in adiponectin levels likely reflect low energy availability in patients with a decreased fat mass.
paragraphs.heading: in AN

paragraphs.text: Recent reports have demonstrated abnor malities in appetite regulatory peptides in women with AN, and ongoing research on these proteins is leading to a greater under standing of the underlying pathophysiology of AN. Ghrelin, an orexigenic hormone, is elevated in adolescents and adults with AN and appears to be positively associated with physical activity [48–50]. Some have even sug gested that ghrelin may serve as a possible biomarker of AN or a promising therapeutic target [51]. Studies of peptide YY (PYY), an anorexigenic peptide released by the gut, have shown conflicting results, with both elevated [52] and normal levels [53] observed in women with AN. The fat-regulated hormones, ghrelin and PYY, appear to signal energy availability to the hypothalamus and may contribute to decreased gonadotropin pulsatility, hypotha lamic amenorrhea, and ultimately lower bone mass [54, 55]. Furthermore, higher PYY levels may directly inhibit osteoblast activity. Recent animal data suggest that new neuropeptides, such as Neuropeptide W, Neuropeptide B, and Vaspin, may be of some importance in the diagnosis and outcome of AN, but their exact roles in humans are still unknown [56].
paragraphs.heading: in AN

paragraphs.text: Elevated serum GH concentrations are found in at least one-half of emaciated patients with AN [57, 58], and these levels return to normal with weight gain [59]. Serum concentrations of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) are suppressed, indicating a state of acquired GH resistance, and levels normalize after nutri tional therapy [60]. This GH resistance was not overcome in a trial of supraphysiologic recombinant human GH administration in women with AN, resulting in persistently low IGF-1, although the women exhibited an increase in lean body mass after treatment [61]. However, a small trial of supplemental GH in young adolescents with prolonged AN showed improvement in height velocity when administered for over 6 months [62]. GH resistance has been attributed to consequences of starvation, but data are conflicting regard ing the relative contributions of severity of weight loss and caloric deprivation.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: Whereas increased basal levels of GH rep resent a reasonably consistent finding in ema ciated patients with AN, GH responses to provocative and suppression tests have been less consistent [60]. Patients with AN exhibit impaired GH responses to l-dopa and apo morphine administration, and two classic studies showed that these findings persist even after nutritional rehabilitation [63]. However, the GH response to arginine has been reported as normal in one study [64]. Furthermore, a paradoxical increase in GH secretion follow ing a glucose load has been reported [65]. In adolescents with AN, GH concentrations fol lowing an oral glucose load suppress to a lesser extent than in normal-weight controls [66]. GH resistance in AN and low IGF-1 lev els are deleterious to bone health as both GH and IGF-1 are osteoanabolic.
Thyroid function tests are abnormal in many patients with AN and likely reflect an adap
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: tive response to permit conservation of energy. Serum levels of T4 and T3 [25] in these patients are significantly lower than in normal individuals. In AN, as in starvation, periph eral deiodination of T4 is diverted from for mation of active T3 to production of reverse T3 (rT3), an inactive metabolite [67]. Levels of T3 correlate linearly with body weight, expressed as a percentage of ideal [68], and normalize with weight gain [69]. Higher levels of rT3, the less active form of the hormone, may explain the occurrence of hypothyroid symptoms, such as fatigue, constipation, and hypothermia, which occur commonly in these patients despite normal to slightly subnormal T4 levels. Levels of thyroid-stimulating hor mone (TSH) are within normal limits [69] and are not related to body weight in AN [69]. However, peak TSH response to thyroidreleasing hormone (TRH) stimulation appears to be delayed (e.g., to 120 min) [70] and may be augmented [68], suggestive of a hypotha lamic defect. The severity of depressive symp toms in these patients has been shown to correlate with lower free T3 concentrations and inhibited conversion from T4 (as assessed by the free T3/free T4 ratio) [71].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: Amenorrhea is historically one of the cardinal features of AN and is due to hypogonado tropic hypogonadism. Studies show markedly underweight patients with AN have low plasma gonadotropin levels [58]. A positive relationship between resting luteinizing hor mone (LH) levels and body weight has been shown, and LH levels normalize with weight gain [72]. Classic studies of 24-h secretory patterns of gonadotropins demonstrate that significant weight loss induces a pattern of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and LH secretion resembling that of prepubertal or early pubertal girls [73]. The pattern is charac terized by either low LH levels throughout the day or decreased LH secretory episodes dur ing waking hours. The LH response to
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian Axis Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) may also be significantly reduced in these patients. The response is correlated with body weight, such that patients with the greatest weight loss have the lowest rise in LH in response to GnRH [72].
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian Axis Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: Weight loss by itself does not completely explain the relationship between nutritional deprivation and disturbances in menstrual function, as amenorrhea precedes significant weight loss in half to two-thirds of patients [58] and may persist despite weight restora tion [74]. Return of menstruation in patients with AN correlates with regaining weight, although not all patients will recover menses with weight gain [75]. A number of investiga tors have identified mean thresholds associ ated with reestablishment of menses in girls with AN based upon estimates of percentages of body fat using height and weight measure ments [76], percentage of ideal body weight [77], and body mass index (BMI) [78]. Resumption of menses has been reported when the percentage of body fat is ≥20% [79, 80], and it is associated in general with the amount of percentage body fat as assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) [81]. The majority of patients resume men struation when weight has returned to at least 90% of ideal [59, 77], in accordance with the work of Frisch and colleagues [76], which demonstrates that the onset and continuation of regular menstrual function in women requires maintenance of a minimal weight for height. However, resumption of menses does not show a simple relationship with weight or body fat [82], and changes in body composi tion do not always predict menstrual recovery. Golden and colleagues noted that even with restoration of normal body weight, amenor rhea may persist in some patients, associated with low leptin levels [83]. In one recent study of women with prolonged amenorrhea despite weight restoration, Arimura and colleagues identified high baseline serum cortisol level as predictive of delayed restoration of menses [84]. In contrast, another study found that higher baseline cortisol predicted greater sub sequent increases in fat mass and leptin, which is turn predicted menstrual recovery [85]. Following weight restoration and resumption
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian Axis Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: of menses, patients with AN appear to have normal fertility [75], although this has not been well-studied. Hypogonadism in AN is a major contributor to low bone density in these patients.
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian Axis Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: Fasting morning concentrations of prolactin are normal in adolescents and women with AN [69, 86], and there is no relationship between basal prolactin and body weight, estradiol, or gonadotropins [69]. Night-time prolactin levels may be reduced, possibly sec ondary to dietary factors as nocturnal prolac tin is reduced by a vegetarian diet in healthy, normal-weight subjects [87], and there is an association of vegetarianism and restrictive eating patterns.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: Several case reports have described disor dered osmoregulation in patients with AN [88, 89]. Partial diabetes insipidus has been reported [86], as have abnormally high cere brospinal fluid (CSF) arginine vasopressin (AVP) levels [90]. A recent case report docu mented the development of central diabetes insipidus during refeeding [89]. There is dis crepancy regarding the levels of oxytocin in patients with AN. Patients with AN have been shown to have decreased serum and CSF oxy tocin concentrations [91, 92] along with reduced responses to stimulation [91]. However, another study showed increased serum levels of oxytocin in malnourished AN patients [93]. Thus, the role for this pituitary hormone in the underlying pathogenesis of AN is unclear.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in AN

paragraphs.text: includes profound deficits of both trabecular and cortical bone compartments [95] with spine bone density reported to be >2 SD below normal in 50% of young women with this disease in one study. The bone loss is so severe that clinical fractures at multiple sites have been documented in women during late adolescence and young adulthood [95–99]. The multiple hormonal alterations which ulti mately contribute to bone loss in AN, includ ing increased bone resorption and decreased bone formation, are summarized in Fig. 33.1.
paragraphs.heading: and Abnormalities in Skeletal Dynamics

paragraphs.text: An uncoupling of bone formation and bone resorption is observed in adult women with AN [100], while adolescents with AN demonstrate a decrease in markers of both bone formation and bone resorption [101], with multifactorial mechanisms contributing to these changes and to bone loss. Although estrogen deficiency is characteristic, estrogen therapy alone does not result in significant increases in bone density. Klibanski and col leagues reported a positive effect of combined estrogen and progestin therapy on bone den sity only in young women who were <70% of

ideal body weight, with no effect on bone den sity for the group as a whole [102]. Oral con traceptives containing both estrogen and progestin are generally not adequate to halt the bone loss seen in AN [103, 104]. This has been attributed to the IGF-1 suppressive effect of oral ethinyl estradiol in oral contra ceptives from hepatic first pass metabolism (as IGF-1 is bone trophic), as well as an increase in sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) lev els, with a decrease in bioavailable levels of gonadal steroids [105]. There also appear to be a direct effect of undernutrition on bone, as levels of IGF-1 (a marker of nutritional status) are subnormal in AN and correlate with markers of bone formation [106, 107]. Misra and colleagues have studied short-term recombinant human (rh) IGF-1 therapy in adolescents with AN for its potential effect on bone density and found that after 7–9 days of treatment, the girls had increases in surrogate markers of bone formation [108]. Furthermore, a randomized, controlled trial of combination therapy with an oral contra ceptive and rhIGF-1 in women with AN dem onstrated modest gains in bone mineral density over 9 months [109]. In contrast to the use of oral estrogen and progestin (as in oral contraceptives), recent studies have shown that physiologic estrogen replacement using transdermal estradiol (with a cyclic progestin) does result in improvements in bone density in adolescents and young adult women with AN after 12–18 months, with bone accrual rates matching or exceeding those in healthy con trols [110, 111]. However, the administration of rhIGF-1 in replacement doses to adoles cents and young adults also receiving trans dermal estradiol did not result in additional benefits beyond those observed with transder mal estradiol alone [112]. Importantly, the use of transdermal estradiol with cyclic progestin is not associated with a decrease in IGF-1 or an increase in SHBG [105].

Deficiencies in androgens, notably DHEA, have also been demonstrated in some studies [23, 113], which may be clinically significant as DHEA appears to have both anabolic and antiosteolytic effects on bone [107, 114]. As noted earlier, our group demonstrated that combined therapy with DHEA and a com
bined oral contraceptive pill preserves BMD and favorably alters hip bone cross-sectional geometry in older adolescents and young women with AN [28, 29] (but not in younger adolescents with AN [30].

Finally, while some studies have demon strated that bisphosphonate treatment reduces bone turnover and increases bone mineral density in adolescents and adults with AN [115, 116], a better understanding of the longterm risks of bisphosphonates is required before these drugs can be considered as part of routine care for use in this population. At the present time, these agents should be used with extreme caution and only under the guid ance of a skeletal health expert [55].

A relatively new area of investigation is the contribution of bone-fat interactions to skel etal remodeling. The bone marrow cavity con tains significant fat tissue which may modulate bone remodeling [117]. Mesenchymal stem cells within bone marrow differentiate to become adipocytes or osteoblasts, driven by hormonal signals [118]. Adipocytes secrete cytokines and adipokines that may either stimulate or inhibit adjacent osteoblasts. Differentiated bone cells secrete factors that influence insulin sensitivity, and fat cells synthesize cytokines that regulate osteoblast differentiation; thus, the two pathways are closely interrelated. States of malnutrition, such as restrictive eating disorders, have been shown to increase marrow adiposity accom panying concurrent losses of subcutaneous adipose tissue, and there is an inverse associa tion between marrow fat and areal BMD mea sures in adults with AN [119, 120]. In adolescents and young women with AN, increased marrow fat has been documented to be present in the peripheral skeleton [121], as well as lumbar spine [120]. A recent crosssectional study in adult women with AN found bone marrow adipose tissue to be directly correlated with fracture history [122]. Further research is needed to understand the relation between marrow adiposity and the etiology of fractures in this disease.
A final new area of research has focused on the effect of restricted eating on bone health in youth who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender [8]. Youth are of high

concern who identify as transgender females. This patient group has recently emerged as a risk group for AN, as these adolescents may be restricting to control pubertal progression or to manifest a slimmer body habitus which can be accompanied by a low bone mass, even prior to pubertal blockade [123].

Patients in whom AN is suspected should undergo a careful patient and family history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and mental health and nutritional assessment. The patient history should focus on weight changes, self-perception of weight and desired weight, a history of bingeing and out-ofcontrol cycles of eating and purging, and uses of laxatives, ipecac, and diet pills. Purging can include hyperexercising. Triggers for weight loss should also be investigated, such as teas ing at school or comments about weight that occurred either in the home or school setting. A careful history around the issues of growth, pubertal progression or delay, and menstrual history is critical as children and adolescents with AN may have delayed puberty and impaired growth and girls may have delayed menarche, amenorrhea, or oligomenorrhea. A family history should include information about eating disorders, obesity, thyroid dis ease, depression, alcoholism, substance abuse, or other evidence of mental illness.
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.9 Patient Evaluation

paragraphs.text: A review of systems should include ques tions about abdominal pain, bloating, consti pation, esophagitis associated with bulimia, hair loss or texture change associated with AN, cold intolerance, fatigue, weakness, faint ing, substance use, and depression. The level of athletic participation and hours per day of physical exercise should be obtained. Special note should be made of previous stress frac tures that may reflect an underlying low bone density for age. One should consider that it is often difficult to distinguish classic AN from the “female athlete triad” (also referred to as “relative energy deficiency in sports” (RED- S)) [124] which includes low energy availabil ity, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone

density [124, 125]. The important underlying concept is that physically active adolescents and young women can develop an energy defi cit that prevents normal hormonal secretion and dynamics that ultimately manifest as alterations in monthly menstrual periods. Adolescent girls with this triad are at increased risk for developing stress fractures, not only because of skeletal deficits but also because of an altered pain threshold, including an inabil ity to stop exercising and rest with the onset of pain.

A dietary history should include a 24-h recall of intake. The amounts may be inaccu rate because teenagers with AN often over report their intake. Triggers of bingeing, such as stress, are important to address. Calcium and vitamin D intake should be estimated by determining the number of servings of dairy products per day or the use of calcium or vita min D supplements. This assessment is help ful in planning treatment interventions to assure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake. It is also important to ask about con sumption of caffeine-containing beverages, as these may decrease a patient’s appetite and increase heart rate at the time of medical eval uations. Documentation of soda consump tion is important as reports suggest an association between consumption of these beverages and fractures in healthy adolescent girls [126–128]. Adolescents can also use excessive consumption of caffeinated soda as a means to suppress appetite and increase their heart rate to meet hemodynamic outpa tient criteria at medical appointments.

The physical examination should include vital signs to assess bradycardia, hypotension, orthostasis, and hypothermia. Weight and height should be recorded in a gown and after urination, so that measurements are consis tent between visits. Heights and weights should be plotted on age-appropriate growth charts to determine the patient’s weight for height and BMI. The urine-specific gravity should be measured since these patients often water load, and abnormalities of vasopressin (e.g., partial diabetes insipidus) have been reported [86]. During the skin examination, the clinician should assess for lanugo hair, dry

skin, hypercarotenemia, hair changes, and calluses on the dorsum of the fingers (Russell’s sign, indicative of bulimic behaviors). The abdomen is typically scaphoid with palpable stool on abdominal exam. Other findings include breast atrophy, hypoestrogenic vagi nal mucosa, and cool and wasted extremities. The cardiac examination should include an assessment for bradycardia, arrhythmias, and mitral valve prolapse. From chronic vomiting, there may be dental caries [129] or acid ero sion of the anterior teeth and parotid hyper trophy. Regular oral health visits are important as dental practitioners are often able to detect the early manifestations of an eating disorder from both dental and gingival signs and changes.

In assessing the history and physical exam ination of an adolescent with suspected AN, the possibility of other diagnoses must be entertained: malignancy, central nervous sys tem tumor, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease and other causes of malabsorption, diabetes mellitus, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, hypopituitarism, primary adrenal insuffi ciency, primary depression (with secondary anorexia), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), among others. The typical labo ratory evaluation obtained at the initial visit includes a complete blood count, differential, sedimentation rate, urinalysis, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and thyroid function tests. If persistent or unex plained amenorrhea is present, serum levels of FSH, LH, and prolactin are obtained before initiation of hormonal replacement therapy. If a patient is sexually active, a urine pregnancy test is obtained. An electrocardio gram is also obtained if the patient is brady cardic or will be using a medication with cardiac side effects. CNS imaging should be considered in a patient with an early or unusual presentation of an eating disorder, growth failure, pubertal arrest, laboratory results consistent with central hypothyroid ism, or neurologic signs and symptoms. Other tests, including endocrinologic assessments, may be considered depending on the patient’s presentation.

There are limited evidenced-based guidelines for the treatment of AN, and treatment guide lines often rely upon expert recommendations [130]. Clinical experience suggests that a mul tidisciplinary team approach can be helpful. A physician typically assumes the role as a manager of the team, performing vital sign and weight checks and coordinating the over all communication with the family. An endo crinologist may address specific endocrinologic issues, such as the amenorrhea and bone loss commonly seen in these patients. A nutrition ist works with the adolescent and family around meal planning and recommendations for caloric requirements and calcium intake. A psychotherapist provides individual and/or family therapy.
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.10 Management

paragraphs.text: The indications for hospitalizations include unstable vital signs, hypotension, orthostasis, bradycardia, severe malnutrition (≤75% ideal body weight), dehydration, abnormal electrolytes, arrhythmias, acute food refusal, uncontrollable bingeing and purging, suicidality, and failure of outpatient therapy. Treatment options include medical hospitalization, psychiatric hospitalization, and day treatment psychiatric programs.
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.10 Management

paragraphs.text: Osteoporosis is a significant health risk for adolescents with AN and often becomes a long-term follow-up issue for an endocrinol ogist [131]. The bone loss and resulting low bone density are often irreversible and may be a source of both short- and long-term morbidity. The degree of bone loss has been associated with duration of both disease and amenorrhea. As short a period as 6 months of estrogen deficiency may have a negative impact on bone density. Other factors to con sider include inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake, hypercortisolism, and adrenal androgen deficiency. The most important approach to the prevention and treatment of low bone mass in AN is the restoration of a normal body weight. Hotta and colleagues [78] found that BMI > 16.4 ± 0.3 kg/m2 was associated with an improvement in bone min eral density. Return of menses, which may occur near a mean of >92 ± 7% of ideal body
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.10 Management

paragraphs.text: weight [77], is an important milestone imply ing the provision of normal estrogen levels to all tissues, including the potential to improve bone mass. Hormonal therapies have been tested with mixed results. At this time, prom ising possibilities include a combination of estrogen, progestin, and DHEA replacement or gonadal steroids and IGF-1 to limit BMD loss in older adolescents and adults with AN. In younger adolescents, transdermal estradiol replacement (with a cyclic progestin for 10 days per month) yielded near-normal bone accrual over a period of 18 months [110], and in a subsequent trial, the addition of IGF-1 to transdermal estradiol did not show an added skeletal benefit [112]. Another trial showed that with physiologic transder mal estradiol replacement (and cyclic oral progesterone 10 days/month), bone accrual improved in adolescents and young adults with AN, approximating those observed in healthy control subjects (who received no intervention) [111]. This regimen also resulted in beneficial changes in cortical min eral density and volumetric BMD as well as failure load at the radius in AN (compared to normal-weight controls). For some patients who have reached their ideal weight but still have not had a return of menses, short-term (i.e., 4–6 months) estrogen monotherapy may be helpful to replete estrogen stores, particu larly in those young women who show no withdrawal bleed in response to a progestin challenge (medroxyprogesterone acetate, 5–10 mg daily for 10 days) [55]. Provision of
paragraphs.heading: 33.1.10 Management

paragraphs.text: adequate calcium and vitamin D intake is important during the critical period for bone accretion. These patients should receive 1300 mg of elemental calcium and 600 inter national units of vitamin D daily [55, 132], although appropriate supplementation doses are debated. Physical activity is associated with increased bone formation [133], and exercise regimens should be individually tai lored to take into account hemodynamic sta bility, level of fitness, and extent of bone loss. Excessive physical activity can exacerbate weight loss and activity levels should be mon itored closely.

Patients with AN exhibit multiple endocrino logic abnormalities. Most of the abnormali ties noted are an adaptive response to starvation and reverse with weight restora tion. Bone loss with potential osteoporosis appears to be the only potentially irreversible endocrinologic abnormality cited to date. Research is clearly needed to understand the multifactorial etiology of disordered eating in adolescents and to develop strategies to pro mote healthy eating patterns in young people. In addition, given that the bone loss seen is often irreversible, future research will hope fully elucidate mechanisms behind this com plication and continue to provide guidance as to new treatment strategies for these young women.

Over 35% of children and adolescents have overweight or obesity, with 19% having obesity, and the prevalence does not appear to be plateauing [134]. Obesity disproportionately affects non- Hispanic black and Hispanic children com pared to non-Hispanic white children [134]. Adolescents have the highest rate of obesity in childhood, with 21% of adolescents having

paragraphs.text: Janet’s laboratory results are classic for a restrictive eating disorder. Reassuring is the fact that electrolytes are normal, as hypokale mia could reflect chronic purging (i.e., selfinduced vomiting). Her glucose is low normal, transaminases are slightly elevated, and the lipid panel is altered (with elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides). Low total T3 and low normal T4 and TSH represent the “euthyroid sick” pattern. DHEAS is low for age. The constellation of results reflects an underlying adaptation to starvation. The appropriate next step would be for the pediatrician to refer the patient to a multidisciplinary program that would pro vide medical, nutritional, and psychological support for this young adolescent, ideally with a family-based component that would provide additional guidance and support for her caretakers. While she is not hemodynami cally unstable to the extent that immediate hospitalization would be warranted, her bor derline bradycardia and hypotension suggest the need for an immediate referral. Longterm evaluation would include DXA screen ing given the history of stress fracture and amenorrhea.

paragraphs.text: obesity compared to 13% of preschoolers [134]. The accumulation of adiposity during puberty contributes to the development of multiple metabolic and endocrinologic abnor malities. Adolescents are growing rapidly and progressing through pubertal changes and, therefore, teleologically are programmed for efficiency in fuel utilization in preparation for the reproductive phase in life. Therefore, when adolescents gain excess weight and develop obesity, the physiologic insulin resistance and high levels of growth hormone, estrogens, and androgens lead to pathologic insulin resis tance and resultant abnormalities in glycemia, lipids, liver function, musculoskeletal func tioning, and reproductive function. In addi tion, adolescents with obesity demonstrate an endocrine profile that in some aspects is the polar opposite from AN but with some over

paragraphs.text: lapping features including amenorrhea, altered growth hormone values, hypercorti solemia, and an altered appetite and meta bolic rate due to alterations in central signalling pathways. In some cases, the abnor malities are the direct opposite of those pres ent in the starvation state of AN, but obesity also represents a pathologic state of excess adiposity resulting in activation of other com pensatory mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: Childhood obesity is a multifactorial condi tion impacted by the perinatal environment, genetics and epigenetic changes, early child hood nutrition, food quality, hypothalamic weight regulation, levels of physical activity, and, in some cases, medical conditions and underlying syndromes. Environmental effects on obesity were acutely displayed during the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in a substantial increase in weight gain and pediat ric obesity prevalence [137]. Genetic evalua tion of obesity for associated phenotypes such as intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, or organ abnormalities has shown a diagnos tic yield of over 40% for a monogenic cause of obesity [138]. However, most children with obesity do not have syndromic features. While several monogenic causes of obesity have been identified [139, 140], even the most com mon melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) vari ants account for <5% of obesity cases in most published series. Therefore, childhood obesity is primarily polygenic, and the heritability of obesity is estimated to be as high as 40% and 70% [141, 142]. There is also increasing evi dence that perinatal and early childhood fac
tors may contribute to epigenetic changes that impact the risk of obesity in later life.

GLP-1 activate pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, causing the synthesis of POMC. POMC is then cleaved by proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1 (PCSK1) to form α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH). α-MSH is released from the nerve terminals in the paraventricular hypothala mus and binds to MC4Rs which cause a reduction in appetite. Serotonin and dopa mine systems also impact weight regulation, having roles in the hypothalamus as well as other brain areas associated with hedonic, or reward related, aspects of eating. Thus, obe sity is caused by an imbalance in energy intake and energy expenditure but is far more com plex than a simple scale imbalance.

Once obesity is established, attempts to reduce energy intake to improve obesity are accompanied by a resultant reduction in energy expenditure, preventing weight loss and increasing the need to further reduce energy intake [145]. This has also been vali dated through mathematical modeling algo rithms [146]. Additionally, the hormone profile after weight loss favors high hunger, with increased pro-orexigenic hormones and decreased anorexigenic hormones [147]. Thus, sustained weight loss has been very difficult to achieve in most patients.

Although obesity is defined by BMI, simi lar BMI in different children can cause very different metabolic and endocrinologic effects. For example, adipose tissue that is deposited in the abdominal cavity, termed visceral adi posity, has a more metabolically unfavorable effect compared to adipose tissue deposited under the skin or subcutaneous adiposity. Thus, individuals who tend to accumulate adi pose tissue centrally with increased visceral fat tend to have more metabolic and endocri nologic abnormalities for the same BMI and overall percentage of body fat.
Metabolic Syndrome. Obesity, the accumula tion of adipocytes, creates an inflammatory condition that along with insulin resistance
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.3 Metabolic Complications

paragraphs.text: results in a series of features termed the meta bolic syndrome. The metabolic syndrome [148] was first defined by Reaven [148] as a list of criteria that all increase risk for cardiovas cular disease in adults. This included elevated insulin, altered glucose tolerance, hyperten sion, low HDL, and elevated triglycerides. The World Health Organization [149], the International Diabetes Federation [150, 151], the National Cholesterol Education Panel Adult Treatment Panel [152], and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) [153] have all proposed definitions for the met abolic syndrome, and they have been adapted over time based on changes in criteria for altered glycemia. These features vary greatly among individuals and between different eth nic groups.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.3 Metabolic Complications

paragraphs.text: Multiple criteria have been proposed for the metabolic syndrome in the pediatric popu lation, and thus there is a lack of consensus for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome in adolescents. Many definitions of metabolic syndrome, including the most commonly cited one by the International Diabetes Foundation, use waist circumference as a criterion instead of BMI measurements. While the guidelines in children use a waist circumference ≥90th percentile, there is some evidence that there are racial differences in these cutoffs [154].

paragraphs.text: Other comorbidities. Obesity is a known risk factor in children for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, dyslip idemia, polycystic ovary syndrome, metabolic

paragraphs.text: (dysfunction) associated steatotic liver disease (formerly called non-alcoholic fatty liver dis ease), and orthopaedic abnormalities (pes pla nus, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, Blount disease). Importantly, these diseases are not just present in late adolescence but are preva lent in primary/elementary school children and even earlier [157]. Even type 2 diabetes, previously thought to be only a postpuberty disease, can be seen in young children before puberty [158]. Some of these disorders, for example type 2 diabetes, appear to progress more rapidly and result in earlier complica tions when compared to adult-onset disease [159, 160]. Thus, earlier screening and inter vention is key to improving the ultimate health of these individuals.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.3 Metabolic Complications

paragraphs.text: In obesity, there may be some degree of over production of cortisol [161] termed pseudo- Cushing syndrome. The enzyme 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1 is present in adipose tissue and converts cortisone to corti sol; thus, this may contribute to the increased cortisol in individuals with obesity. Further, increased excretion of cortisol in urine con tributes to higher than typical 24-h urinary cortisol concentrations. Pathogenic hypercor tisolism, termed Cushing Syndrome, results in central obesity, a full, round face, muscle atro phy and slowing of linear growth in children who have not yet reached final adult stature. In association with the central adiposity, patients can present with metabolic abnor malities including hyperglycemia, hyperlipid emia, and hypertension. Therefore, this syndrome can phenotypically overlap with obesity associated with metabolic abnormali ties.
paragraphs.heading: Adrenal (HPA) Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Distinguishing between the two disorders is important. Mild elevations of cortisol in obesity have no clear detrimental effects and are not treated. On the other hand, Cushing’s syndrome requires treatment of the underly ing cause of hypercortisolism. The gold stan

dard test to diagnose Cushing syndrome is a 24-h urinary collection for free cortisol, with further evaluation necessary if at least two 24-h cortisol concentrations are elevated. However, given the difficulty in obtaining 24-h urinary collections, other proposed tests to distinguish these two entities have included midnight serum and/or late night salivary cor tisol assessments and dexamethasone-CRH testing [162, 163]. The Pituitary Society prac tice guidelines suggest that first-line testing include 24-h urinary free cortisol, midnight salivary cortisol, or 1 mg overnight dexameth asone suppression tests. Although mild eleva tions are most likely to be the result of pseudo-Cushing in an adolescent with obe sity, it is important not to miss the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome, so in some cases fur ther evaluation and/or a referral to an endo crinologist is warranted.

Premature adrenarche, discussed more in Chap. 26, is more common in children with obesity [164] as are increases in DHEAS [165]. Changes in enzyme expression in the zona reticularis lead to increased production of DHEAS and other steroid hormones, such as androstenedione and testosterone [166]. Diagnostic workup for pathogenic causes of premature adrenarche includes obtaining a bone age. Typically, if the bone age is <2SD above the child’s chronologic age, the signs of adrenarche are considered benign, and no fur ther workup is needed. However, a signifi cantly advanced bone age is commonly seen in individuals with premature adrenarche who have higher BMI and are taller [167]. Thus, using a criteria of a bone age > 2SD above the height age (the age corresponding to the child’s height when it is equal to the 50th per centile) may be a more useful criteria in chil dren with obesity and premature pubarche/ adrenarche.
Insulin has different weight-related effects depending on its location of action. Within the brain, insulin acts as a satiety signal,
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: decreasing food intake through action in the hypothalamus [168]. However, insulin is also an extremely important inhibitor of lipolysis, thus promoting adipose tissue accumulation both directly at the level of the adipocyte and within the brain [169, 170]. In obesity, there is often, but not always, an increase in insulin levels. However, the increase in inflammation that also accompanies excess adipose tissue results in insulin resistance. Thus, satiating effects of increased insulin are not observed in obesity.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: As mentioned above, leptin, discovered in 1994 and a product of the LEP gene (initially termed the ob gene in mice), is secreted by adi pocytes, and provides a signal to the central nervous system that adipose tissue is present. Leptin levels are correlated with the degree of obesity. Leptin receptors are present in the central nervous system in the hypothalamic regions known to regular hunger and satiety but are also present on various organs. Leptin deficiency results in severe, early onset obesity due to a lack of satiety [171]. Therefore, ele vated leptin levels in obesity should provide a protective mechanism against excessive adi pose accumulation by reducing appetite and reducing adiposity. However, this does not occur in those with obesity. Thus, there is some degree of leptin resistance that develops in obesity allowing for increased hunger in the setting of increased leptin. Interestingly, leptin is likely a major reason for elevated blood pressure in obesity [172].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Adiponectin is an adipocytokine that has protective metabolic effects. Elevated levels of adiponectin decrease the risk of myocardial infarction in adult men [173]. Unfortunately, instead of increasing as adipose tissue expands, adiponectin levels become lower as obesity increases in children and adolescents [174]. Low levels of adiponectin are predictive of adult type 2 diabetes [175], hypertension [176] and are associated in children with higher C-reactive protein and components of the metabolic syndrome [177].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Ghrelin, a known orexigenic hormone, is decreased in children with obesity and increases with weight loss [50, 53]. Thus, while ghrelin is likely not a causative agent in the
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: development of obesity, it likely plays a role in the failure of individuals to maintain weight loss.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Obesity in childhood prior to puberty is asso ciated with taller stature than normal-weight peers [178, 179]. This seemingly obesityinduced height gain is attenuated in puberty, thus childhood obesity is not associated with taller stature in adulthood [178, 179]. Therefore, there appears to be an effect of excess adipose tissue on growth moderated by other hormonal milieu.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Interestingly, most studies, including a recent metaanalysis, have concluded that obe sity results in reduced basal and stimulated growth hormone levels [180–182]. Growth hormone levels in the range used to diagnose growth hormone deficiency are present in adults with obesity and are associated with increased dysmetabolic profiles and metaboli cally unfavorable adipose tissue distribution, including increased visceral adiposity [183, 184]. In fact, some studies have suggested that visceral adiposity (more than overall weight or body mass index) is associated with lower growth hormone levels [185, 186]. This asso ciation of low growth hormone levels with obesity is not surprising given that conditions causing primary growth hormone deficiency typically have increased adiposity, particu larly visceral adiposity, as a prominent fea ture. Reduced growth hormone secretion can be reversed with weight loss [187], supporting likely interactions between adipokines and the pituitary.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Obesity induces a reduction in growth hor mone secretion from the pituitary gland, but studies are mixed as to whether this results in a decrease, increase, or no change in total IGF-1 and/or free IGF-1 levels. This is an important practical point, as IGF-1 is often used to screen for growth hormone status, and growth hormone stimulation tests used to diagnose growth hormone deficiency in chil dren categorize significantly more children at
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: a higher (versus lower) BMI with growth hor mone deficiency [188]. This may also be influ enced by age as a recent study has shown younger children with obesity have higher IGF-1 levels, but during puberty these levels are decreased compared to peers [178].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: The mechanisms that induce a reduction in growth hormone secretion in obesity are likely multifactorial and interrelated. The reduction in growth hormone may occur due to hyperinsulinemia, resulting in negative feedback on growth hormone production [189]. Other theories suggest that it is related to the hyperinsulinemia suppressing insulin-like growth factor-binding protein-1 (IGFBP-1), which, in term, modifies the free IGF-1 available and thus suppresses growth hormone secretion. However, studies are inconclusive when free IGF-1 is measured in the setting of obesity or acute overfeeding [190–192]. Some studies have suggested that free fatty acids are a primary factor in reduc tion of growth hormone levels in obesity. Free fatty acids are known to suppress growth hor mone production and are increased in obesity [193]. In an experimental design, the use of a medication known to reduce free fatty acids resulted in improved growth hormone secre tion in adults with obesity [194]. Free fatty acids may have a direct effect or act through somatostatin to decrease growth hormone in obesity [195]. Changes in ghrelin, a gutderived peptide that stimulates hunger and binds to the growth hormone secretagogue receptor and is lower in children with obesity compared to their normal-weight peers, may also play a role in the impact of obesity on growth hormone [196].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: As noted above in the discussion of the adrenal axis, 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydro genase is present in adipose tissue and con verts cortisone to cortisol. Growth hormone plays a role in inhibiting this activity. Therefore, the reduction in growth hormone may also contribute to the increase in cortisol which then increases adiposity [197]. Therefore, the obesity induced reduction in growth hormone levels, like the increase in

insulin levels, may induce a vicious cycle, pro moting additional weight gain and increased adiposity, particularly visceral adiposity. Thus, it remains unclear whether the reduc tion in growth hormone secretion is a physio logic metabolically favorable development, inducing a reduction in glycemia, or an unfa vorable development, increasing visceral adi posity through reduced lipolysis and increasing inflammatory mediators. Supplementation of growth hormone or its stimulatory factors in obesity remains an area of active investigation.

A mildly elevated TSH is often present in obe sity, causing clinical confusion as to whether this mild degree of compensated hypothyroid ism is a causative factor in the development of obesity or whether it is a result of weight gain. In general, only profound hypothyroidism causes rapid weight gain, and therefore, the mild TSH elevation in obesity is likely a con sequence of weight gain. A clinical clue is that hypothyroidism causes a reduction in linear growth, while obesity often promotes increased linear growth. Adipocytes have deiodinase activity and therefore participate in thyroid hormone metabolism, which may be a factor in these apparent abnormalities. In a study of children with obesity and normalweight children, the known mild elevation in TSH was demonstrated and noted to correlate with BMI, waist circumference, and lipid abnormalities [198]. Although the role of TSH elevations in weight gain is not clear, there are also associations of subclinical hypothyroidism with insulin resistance and multiple cardiometabolic risk factors [199]. Further studies are needed to determine whether mild alterations in thyroid function are causative factors in the metabolic changes seen with obesity. At this time there is no rec ommendation to treat these mild TSH eleva tions in children [200].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Precocious puberty is more prevalent in girls with obesity compared to those of normal weight. This point had been controversial in earlier studies due to the criteria used to eval uate thelarche and concerns that adipose tis sue deposition may have been mistaken for evidence of early puberty. However, welldesigned studies [201–203] have documented earlier onset of both thelarche and menarche in girls with obesity. A more recent study has shown that the increased risk of central preco cious puberty in children with obesity is significant only when obesity has been present for over 2 years [204].
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: The impact of obesity on pubertal devel opment in boys has been less well-studied. However, a large investigation of over 4000 boys demonstrated a correlation between age of pubertal onset by testicular size and BMI. Boys with overweight and obesity were found to begin puberty and progress through puberty at an earlier age [205]. Despite some evidence supporting earlier pubertal progres sion in boys, obesity has also been associated with reductions in testosterone level and increased risk of gynecomastia, both lipomas tia and true breast development. This is thought to be due to the aromatization of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue. Thus, some degree of hypogonadism may be present in some adolescent males with obesity.
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Mechanisms underlying earlier pubertal onset in children with obesity remain an area of active investigation. Leptin is known to be permissive in pubertal initiation and leptin deficiency results in a lack of pubertal changes. Leptin is also elevated in obesity. However, while leptin is permissive for puberty, it is not a causative factor. Additional mechanistic possibilities include hyperinsulinism leading to a suppression in sex hormone-binding globulin and thus increased bioavailability of sex steroids. The impact of androgens being aromatized to estrogens by adipose tissue has
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: also been postulated to play an important role in early pubertal changes in girls and may have variable impact on pubertal changes in boys.
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Early hyperandrogenism and premature adrenarche are also more common in girls with obesity and have been linked in some populations to an increased risk of progres sion to PCOS in adolescence and adulthood [206].
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Obesity also impacts conception and preg nancy/birth complications. High BMI is asso ciated with reduced semen quality [207]. PCOS can impact female fertility and is asso ciated with obesity and insulin resistance (dis cussed in depth in Chap. 28). Obesity during pregnancy increases risks of pre eclampsia, miscarriage, and congenital abnor malities [208].
paragraphs.heading: Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Prolactin, a hormone crucial for lactation, may also regulate energy metabolism [209]. Prolactin levels are increased in adults with overweight or obesity and higher levels are associated with metabolically beneficial pro files [210]. This may be in part due to eleva tions of prolactin being associated with visceral fat mass, a more metabolically detri mental fat depot [211].
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: Oxytocin, another hormone important for lactation but also for normal birth processes, is synthesized in both the brain and the gas trointestinal tract and has important meta bolic actions [212]. Genetic polymorphisms in the oxytocin gene have been linked to obesity in adolescents [213]. Additionally, low oxyto cin levels in adolescents are correlated with higher hyperphagia scores [213], indicating a possible association between satiety and oxy tocin. This association is supported by animal studies which show oxytocin signals through receptors in the brain to activate the POMC pathway and induce satiation [214]; however, it is notable that animal models lacking oxyto
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: cin action develop obesity without hyperpha gia [215]. On the other hand, oxytocin can impact muscle development [216], inhibit the development of adipocytes [217], stimulate lipolysis [218], and promote increased energy expenditure [219]. Small clinical trials have shown that intranasal oxytocin may signifi cantly reduce hunger and/or food intake [220] and possibly reduce BMI [221], which has led to additional clinical trials underway to deter mine the therapeutic usefulness of oxytocin in obese states.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities in Obesity

paragraphs.text: As described in detail above, AN, a condition of extreme underweight and nutritional defi ciency, results in a reduction in bone mineral density. However, the opposite extreme, ele vated weight in obesity also leads to changes in bone density and structure [222]. Most studies, including metaanalyses, show increased bone mineral density in individuals with obesity [223–225]. Despite the reassur ing trends in bone density, children with obe sity may be at increased risk for reduced bone strength [226] and fractures [227, 228]. Increased adiposity may cause alterations at the level of the bone through inflammatory markers and mediators. Furthermore, as adi pocytes and osteoblasts are both derived from a common progenitor mesenchymal stem cell, an alteration in one cell type may contribute to alterations in the other [229]. It is well-documented that 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are lower in individuals with obesity, attributable to both reduced dietary intake and increased distribution in adipose tissue. However, whether or not lower vitamin D levels in children with obesity are associated with fracture risk remains controversial [230, 231].
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.10 Skeletal Impact of Obesity

paragraphs.text: Visceral adiposity, the more metabolically active and detrimental fat depot compared to subcutaneous adiposity, appears to be detri mental to bone health. Higher levels of vis ceral fat have been found to correlate with lower bone density in both adolescent girls [232] and women [233] with obesity.

The evaluation of a child with obesity starts with an analysis of the weight/BMI trajectory over the patient’s life. Physicians should iden tify whether obesity was severe prior to age 5 years, a marker of possible genetic forms of obesity, or whether there were any inflection points marking a significant change that exac erbated weight gain. In general, the medical history evaluation focuses on determining whether or not there are red flags for genetic forms of obesity or undiagnosed comorbidi ties that need to be addressed. Further, the family history should elucidate any strong family history of severe obesity, bariatric sur gery, or other familial disorders (i.e., vision problems, developmental delays, or pregnancy losses). Additionally, a history of consanguin ity in the family increases the risk for genetic disorders. Current medical problems and past medical history may reveal other hints for syndromic features associated with obesity, such as developmental or cognitive delays, learning disabilities, vision difficulties, or organ abnormalities. The review of systems screens for comorbidities such as headaches for pseudotumor cerebri, joint pain for ortho paedic problems, fatigue for obstructive sleep apnea, or polyuria/polydipsia for diabetes. In the physical exam, care is taken to identify signs of comorbidities such as elevated blood pressure, acanthosis, abnormal optic discs, or hepatomegaly. There are several excellent guidelines which give additional detail for the work-up of childhood obesity [234–237].
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Guidelines differ regarding laboratory rec ommendations for childhood obesity. In gen eral, guidelines point to starting screening for obesity comorbidities at age six with an ALT, lipid panel, and haemoglobin A1c, although the recent American Academy of Pediatrics obesity guidelines recommend screening only in those 10 years and older for ALT and abnormal glucose metabolism [238]. However, there is evidence that individuals less than age 6 years can have evidence of obesity-related diseases [239]. Thus, physicians may want to consider testing earlier than the current rec ommendations depending on the specific sce
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

paragraphs.text: nario. Referrals to specialists may be necessary based on the history, physical and laboratory findings to further evaluate obesity-related comorbidities or possible genetic causes of obesity.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Treatment of pediatric obesity is based on lifestyle modifications. Unfortunately, there is little to date to help physicians tailor their advice to specific individuals.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

paragraphs.text: First-line treatment for obesity and related metabolic factors is behavioral change sup ported by family-centered, multidisciplinary treatment in individual and/or group settings. The goal of behavioral change is to imple ment an improved diet, targeting reducing the glycemic index in foods, increasing intake of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins and healthy fats while eliminating sugar containing bever ages and significantly reducing intake of pro cessed carbohydrates. Physical activity with a goal of 60 min daily, including 30 min three times per week of moderate to vigorous activ ity, can improve insulin resistance and the inflammatory profile even without inducing weight loss. The most recent US Preventative Task Force analysis on obesity in children and adolescents states that only comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions with at least 26 contact hours were successful for weight loss [236]. Thus, multi-component and multi-specialty/disciplinary programs are instrumental in the treatment of childhood obesity.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.12 Management

paragraphs.text: Second-line therapies can include medica tions and, in some cases, bariatric surgery. Pharmacotherapy in childhood obesity is underutilized [240], especially given the failure of lifestyle modifications to effectively cause changes at the population level. Expert opin
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.12 Management

paragraphs.text: ion suggests pharmacotherapy initiation could be considered in individuals with obe sity who have not had success with lifestyle interventions and who agree to long-term therapy if efficacy outcomes are met (≥5% BMI reduction from baseline after 12 weeks on optimal dose) [241]. Unfortunately, there are only a small number of pharmacotherapy options available for those at least 12 years of age. The currently approved medications (as of 2023) include orlistat (a lipase inhibitor), liraglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist), sema glutide (a weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist), and phentermine/topiramate (a combination stimulant and anticonvulsant). Orlistat, along with behavioral modification, can induce 19% of subjects to have a 5% or greater weight loss, with 9.5% of subjects losing more than 10% of body weight in clinical trials [242]. Liraglutide resulted in 43% of adolescents attaining a ≥5% BMI change with 26% achiev ing at least 10% BMI loss [243]. At the highest dose, 46% of adolescents taking phentermine/ topiramate achieved at least 5% BMI reduc tion and 42% achieved 10% or more BMI loss [244]. Semaglutide resulted in a 5% or more BMI reduction in 76% of adolescents with obesity, with 63% of subjects experiencing a 10% or more BMI loss [245]. Bariatric surgery is also being performed in adolescents, and in recent published data, the results and side effects appear to be similar to those docu mented in adults when performed at experi enced centers [246]. At 5 years, patients had an average weight reduction of 26%, and over 75% had more than a 20% weight loss. The large majority of patients had resolution of diabetes (86%), hypertension (68%), and hypertriglyceridemia (81%). The most com mon complications were micronutrient defi ciencies with potential implications for bone health, and 20% of patients needed an addi tional abdominal surgical procedure.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.12 Management

paragraphs.text: A 14-year-old girl presents to the endocrinol ogy clinic with the complaints of weight gain and irregular menses. She and her mother report that she has always been “heavy” but that over the last 2 years, she has gained over 20 pounds per year, without any linear growth change. They have noticed darkening of the skin on her neck. She has had worsening facial acne and progressive hirsutism on the face and chest. Her weight has recently stabilized after reducing some of her daily intake of soda and processed snacks. Review of systems is negative except for intermittent headaches (1 per month, typically after school).
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.12 Management

paragraphs.text: She was born at term after a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes, and has intermittent asthma not requiring daily medi cal therapy. She reached menarche at age 10 years but has never had regular menstrual cycles; menses occur every 3–4 months. She is receiving no medications currently, but has required oral glucocorticoid therapy in the past for acute asthma exacerbations. A review of her medical chart shows her BMI was at 121% of the 95th percentile at age 4 and she has tracked between 120–135% of the 95th percentile for most of her life. Her height has been consis tently between the 90th–95th percentile.
paragraphs.heading: 33.2.12 Management

paragraphs.text: Her family history is significant for obesity in her mother, 12-year-old sister, and maternal grandfather. A maternal aunt had bariatric sur gery. Her father has normal weight and no medical problems. Her 10-year-old brother has ADHD and has normal weight. There is no his tory of consanguinity, pregnancy losses, or other disorders in the family.

Her primary care provider noted a BMI of 35 kg/m2 (127% of the 95th percentile) at her 14-year annual physical and was concerned about her elevated BMI and rapid weight gain. She obtained screening laboratory studies to evaluate causative factors and to screen for potential comorbidities. The results are as fol lows:
5 Fasting glucose 104 mg/dL.
5 Fasting insulin 28 uU/mL.
5 AST 46 unit/L.
5 ALT 58 unit/L.
5 Cholesterol 195 mg/dL.
5 LDL 155 mg/dL.
5 Triglycerides 225 mg/dL.
5 HDL 38 mg/dL.
5 TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
7.40 mcunit/mL. 5 Free testosterone 11.1 pg/mL.
5 DHEAS 400 mcg/dL.

The labs include impaired fasting glucose (>100 mg/dL), HbA1C (5.7–6.5%) in the pre diabetes range, and mildly elevated liver enzymes concerning for nonalcoholic steato hepatitis. Her lipid panel demonstrated an elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycer ides and a low HDL. Her TSH was mildly ele vated. Her free testosterone and DHEAS were also elevated. The abnormalities were all con sistent with obesity associated metabolic changes and the related syndrome of polycys tic ovary syndrome. Specifically, she has insu lin resistance as noted by her physical findings of acanthosis nigricans and elevated fasting insulin. She has dysglycemia, as indicated by her impaired fasting glucose and a prediabetes range HbA1C. This along with her history of being the result of a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes and her family history increases her risk for progression to diabetes. She has lipids and liver function studies con sistent with a dysmetabolic state. Her clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism along with her irregular menses are consistent with a clinical diagnosis of PCOS. Her strong family history of obesity and history of severe obe sity from an early age is suspicious for a pos sible genetic form of obesity, such as an MC4R variant. Thus, genetic testing should be dis cussed with the family. All metabolic abnor malities will likely improve with weight loss and a reduction in inflammation and insulin resistance. She should be offered an intensive behavior and lifestyle treatment program and obesity pharmacotherapy should be discussed as an adjunct treatment..

In summary, obesity is a common problem in childhood and results in multiple endocrino logic manifestations. These include changes in glycemia, lipids, and other cardiovascular risk factors. In addition, alterations in cortisol production, thyroid function studies, and growth hormone occur. Bone health and reproductive health are also impacted by adi posity. Primary treatment includes treating the individual with intensive lifestyle manage ment and pharmacotherapy when necessary. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is increas ingly being used in adolescents with moderate to severe obesity.

5 Restrictive eating disorders such as

anorexia nervosa (AN) result in multi ple endocrine alterations with accom panying relative growth hormone resistance and hypercortisolemia due to hyperactivity of the hypothalamic– pituitary–adrenal axis. 5 In AN, thyroid abnormalities represent

a “euthyroid sick” profile and typically normalize with weight gain and psycho logical recovery, without the need for

l-thyroxine replacement. 5 AN results in abnormalities in the

reproductive axis in both boys and girls; girls may develop oligomenorrhea and, more commonly, amenorrhea. 5 Early bone loss and/or lack of bone

accrual are a serious consequence in adolescent girls and boys with AN, with some skeletal losses representing irre versible changes. 5 Obesity results in endocrine changes

including hypercortisolism, altered growth hormone secretion, and mild thyroid axis abnormalities. These often improve with weight loss. 5 Adiposity accumulation and resultant

obesity lead to multiple metabolic changes that increase the risk for future cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabe tes. 5 Obesity results in abnormalities in the
