health, with increased fracture risk in some populations.

### 33.1 Anorexia Nervosa

### 33.1.1 Introduction

Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric and medical condition once described as the “relentless pursuit of thinness” [1]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental

Disorders, fifth edition (DSM-5), was pub lished in 2013 and includes a significantly revised eating disorder section. By the new cri teria, recent prevalence data estimate the rate of AN to be 4% among females and 0.3% among males, with a stable overall incidence rate over the past several decades, but increased incidence among youth <15 years [2]. The disorder is most commonly seen among adolescent girls (i.e., assigned female at birth) of postindustrialized, high-income countries, with estimates that 19–30% of younger patients with AN are male, and the overall prevalence of this disorder among adolescent boys appears to be increasing [3, 4]. Testosterone deficiency and many endo crine alterations seen in girls are also seen in adolescent boys with this diagnosis [5, 6]. The overall prevalence of AN has also risen dra matically since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with both inpatient and outpatient programs seeing a 3–4-fold increase in the prevalence of all restrictive eating disorders compared to prepandemic rates [7]. Another newly identified risk group are lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender youth who fre quently exhibit body image distortion and dis ordered eating [8]. Eighty-five percent of patients with AN present between the ages of 13 and 20 years during a critical period for growth, pubertal development, and maximal bone accretion that culminates in peak bone mass. The disorder can result in a compromise in each of these important endocrinologic events, with lifelong sequelae. Reports over the past decade document an earlier age of onset of AN [9], and it is recognized that onset at a younger age is associated with less opti mal growth and bone health outcomes [10].

Patients with AN also have a characteristic clinical picture of endocrine dysfunction, including amenorrhea, abnormal temperature regulation, elevated growth hormone (GH) levels associated with lower levels of insulin like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), hypercorti solemia, and abnormal eating suggestive of hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction [11]. Therefore, endocrine function has been stud ied extensively in these patients. The multiple endocrine abnormalities appear to represent an adaptation to the starvation state.


## PDF page 890 | printed page 892

The clinical features of AN by DSM-5 criteria are shown as follows. Amenorrhea was excluded as a diagnostic criteria with the DSM-5 publication in 2013 [12]. However, the absence of amenorrhea among the diagnostic criteria should not diminish bone health con cerns in the young woman who manifests all other features. There can still be hormonal alterations at play that pose a risk to bone health despite ongoing menses. Furthermore, despite amenorrhea no longer being required for the diagnosis of AN, a larger proportion of patients with this condition are, in fact, amenorrheic.

DSM-5 Criteria for Anorexia Nervosa

1. Restriction of energy intake relative to

requirements, leading to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health. Significantly low weight is defined as a weight that is less than minimally normal or, for children and adolescents, less than that minimally expected. 2. Intense fear of gaining weight or of

### 33

becoming fat or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight. 3. Disturbance in the way in which one’s

body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

### 33.1.2 Hypothalamic–Pituitary–

### Adrenal Axis in AN

Patients with AN exhibit hyperactivity of their hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis [13–15]. These patients typically have ele vated serum cortisol concentrations, accom panied by increased corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) secretion and normal circu lating levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The elevation in cortisol appears to be secondary to increased cortisol produc

tion, decreased clearance, or a combination of both factors [14]. Boyar and colleagues [16] were the first to report decreased cortisol metabolism in AN, subsequently confirmed by other groups. Walsh and colleagues [17] noted that when body size was taken into account (cortisol production/kg), cortisol secretion was significantly increased.

Overactivity of the HPA axis is largely sec ondary to increased CRH production but with circadian rhythmicity maintained. Adolescents with AN, as compared to healthy controls, have higher cortisol due to increased frequency of secretory bursts, suggesting increased cortisol secretion in this population [18]. Patients with AN may also exhibit inad equate suppression of cortisol after an over night oral dexamethasone challenge [17, 19]. Estour and colleagues [20] administered dexa methasone intravenously to 15 patients with AN and observed nonsuppression in 93%. Results of those studies suggest that the hypercortisolism seen in AN is not suppress ible by exogenous glucocorticoid. The abnor malities appear to improve after refeeding and weight gain. Gold and colleagues [13] found increased cortisol response to CRH, while Hotta and colleagues [21] showed a decreased response. Both the groups interpret their find ings as an indication that there is increased HPA axis activity due to increased CRH secretion in AN. Higher cortisol levels in AN contribute to both reproductive dysfunction and low bone density.

The adrenal androgens dehydroepiandros terone (DHEA) and DHEA sulfate (DHEAS) have been reported to be abnormal in some, although not all, studies in young women with AN. In adult women with AN, DHEAS has been shown to be decreased [22, 23], increased [24], or unchanged [25, 26] as compared to healthy controls. In adolescents with AN, DHEAS inversely correlates with markers of bone resorption [27]. A combination regimen of oral DHEA, estrogen, and progestin was found to be safe and effective for preserving BMD in young women with AN [28]. A fol low-up study showed significant changes in measures of hip strength and cross-sectional geometry in the treated group compared to


## PDF page 891 | printed page 893

placebo that may translate to a lower fracture risk [27, 29]. Of concern, however, a subse quent clinical trial did not show the skeletal benefit of combined adrenal/gonadal hormone replacement that was seen in earlier studies of older adolescents and young women; in fact, a deleterious effect was observed in those with open epiphyses [30]. Thus, there appears to be a differential effect in efficacy among adolescents with open vs. closed epiphyses, limiting the applicability of this therapeutic option for adolescents.

### 33.1.3 Peripheral Metabolic Signals

### in AN

Studies examining the question of insulin dynamics in AN have yielded contradictory results [31], demonstrating both insulin resis tance and insulin deficiency in these patients. Low fasting glucose and insulin concentra tions have been reported in AN [27], as have both normal [32] and increased insulin sensi tivity [33]. Patients with AN have also demon strated subnormal insulin rises after oral dexamethasone compared to healthy, normalweight controls [34]. Thus, adolescents with AN exhibit either an isolated resistance to glucocorticoids at a pancreatic level or com promised pancreatic function after months of starvation, with a diminished ability to respond to high-glucose challenge.

Leptin, a peptide hormone secreted by adipose tissue (e.g., adipokine) that is osteo anabolic, is altered by adaptations to a starva tion state [35]. The subnormal plasma leptin concentrations seen in AN [36] likely reflect the decreased fat mass in these subjects. Subnormal leptin levels in patients with amen orrhea suggest that this hormone may serve as a metabolic signal to the reproductive axis [37–39]. ### 33.1.9 Patient Evaluation

Patients in whom AN is suspected should undergo a careful patient and family history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and mental health and nutritional assessment. The patient history should focus on weight changes, self-perception of weight and desired weight, a history of bingeing and out-ofcontrol cycles of eating and purging, and uses of laxatives, ipecac, and diet pills. Purging can include hyperexercising. Triggers for weight loss should also be investigated, such as teas ing at school or comments about weight that occurred either in the home or school setting. A careful history around the issues of growth, pubertal progression or delay, and menstrual history is critical as children and adolescents with AN may have delayed puberty and impaired growth and girls may have delayed menarche, amenorrhea, or oligomenorrhea. A family history should include information about eating disorders, obesity, thyroid dis ease, depression, alcoholism, substance abuse, or other evidence of mental illness.

### 33.1.10 Management

There are limited evidenced-based guidelines for the treatment of AN, and treatment guide lines often rely upon expert recommendations [130]. Clinical experience suggests that a mul tidisciplinary team approach can be helpful. A physician typically assumes the role as a manager of the team, performing vital sign and weight checks and coordinating the over all communication with the family. An endo crinologist may address specific endocrinologic issues, such as the amenorrhea and bone loss commonly seen in these patients. A nutrition ist works with the adolescent and family around meal planning and recommendations for caloric requirements and calcium intake. A psychotherapist provides individual and/or family therapy.

The indications for hospitalizations include unstable vital signs, hypotension, orthostasis, bradycardia, severe malnutrition (≤75% ideal body weight), dehydration, abnormal electrolytes, arrhythmias, acute food refusal, uncontrollable bingeing and purging, suicidality, and failure of outpatient therapy. Treatment options include medical hospitalization, psychiatric hospitalization, and day treatment psychiatric programs.

Osteoporosis is a significant health risk for adolescents with AN and often becomes a long-term follow-up issue for an endocrinol ogist [131]. The bone loss and resulting low bone density are often irreversible and may be a source of both short- and long-term morbidity. The degree of bone loss has been associated with duration of both disease and amenorrhea. As short a period as 6 months of estrogen deficiency may have a negative impact on bone density. Other factors to con sider include inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake, hypercortisolism, and adrenal androgen deficiency. The most important approach to the prevention and treatment of low bone mass in AN is the restoration of a normal body weight. Hotta and colleagues [78] found that BMI > 16.4 ± 0.3 kg/m2 was associated with an improvement in bone min eral density. Return of menses, which may occur near a mean of >92 ± 7% of ideal body

### 33

Childhood obesity is a multifactorial condi tion impacted by the perinatal environment, genetics and epigenetic changes, early child hood nutrition, food quality, hypothalamic weight regulation, levels of physical activity, and, in some cases, medical conditions and underlying syndromes. Environmental effects on obesity were acutely displayed during the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in a substantial increase in weight gain and pediat ric obesity prevalence [137]. Genetic evalua tion of obesity for associated phenotypes such as intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, or organ abnormalities has shown a diagnos tic yield of over 40% for a monogenic cause of obesity [138]. While several monogenic causes of obesity have been identified [139, 140], even the most com mon melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) vari ants account for <5% of obesity cases in most published series. results in a series of features termed the meta bolic syndrome. The metabolic syndrome [148] was first defined by Reaven [148] as a list of criteria that all increase risk for cardiovas cular disease in adults. This included elevated insulin, altered glucose tolerance, hyperten sion, low HDL, and elevated triglycerides. The World Health Organization [149], the International Diabetes Federation [150, 151], the National Cholesterol Education Panel Adult Treatment Panel [152], and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) [153] have all proposed definitions for the met abolic syndrome, and they have been adapted over time based on changes in criteria for altered glycemia. These features vary greatly among individuals and between different eth nic groups.

Multiple criteria have been proposed for the metabolic syndrome in the pediatric popu lation, and thus there is a lack of consensus for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome in adolescents. Many definitions of metabolic syndrome, including the most commonly cited one by the International Diabetes Foundation, use waist circumference as a criterion instead of BMI measurements. While the guidelines in children use a waist circumference ≥90th percentile, there is some evidence that there are racial differences in these cutoffs [154].

Utilizing NHANES data, [155, 156] pedi atric metabolic syndrome was defined as including three or more of the following:

### 33.2.4 Hypothalamic-Pituitary-

### Adrenal (HPA) Axis in Obesity

In obesity, there may be some degree of over production of cortisol [161] termed pseudo- Cushing syndrome. The enzyme 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1 is present in adipose tissue and converts cortisone to corti sol; thus, this may contribute to the increased cortisol in individuals with obesity. Further, increased excretion of cortisol in urine con tributes to higher than typical 24-h urinary cortisol concentrations. Pathogenic hypercor tisolism, termed Cushing Syndrome, results in central obesity, a full, round face, muscle atro phy and slowing of linear growth in children who have not yet reached final adult stature. In association with the central adiposity, patients can present with metabolic abnor malities including hyperglycemia, hyperlipid emia, and hypertension. Therefore, this syndrome can phenotypically overlap with obesity associated with metabolic abnormali ties.

### 33

Distinguishing between the two disorders is important. Mild elevations of cortisol in obesity have no clear detrimental effects and are not treated. On the other hand, Cushing’s syndrome requires treatment of the underly ing cause of hypercortisolism. The gold stan

dard test to diagnose Cushing syndrome is a 24-h urinary collection for free cortisol, with further evaluation necessary if at least two 24-h cortisol concentrations are elevated. However, given the difficulty in obtaining 24-h urinary collections, other proposed tests to distinguish these two entities have included midnight serum and/or late night salivary cor tisol assessments and dexamethasone-CRH testing [162, 163]. The Pituitary Society prac tice guidelines suggest that first-line testing include 24-h urinary free cortisol, midnight salivary cortisol, or 1 mg overnight dexameth asone suppression tests. Although mild eleva tions are most likely to be the result of pseudo-Cushing in an adolescent with obe sity, it is important not to miss the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome, so in some cases fur ther evaluation and/or a referral to an endo crinologist is warranted.

Premature adrenarche, discussed more in Chap. 26, is more common in children with obesity [164] as are increases in DHEAS [165]. Changes in enzyme expression in the zona reticularis lead to increased production of DHEAS and other steroid hormones, such as androstenedione and testosterone [166]. Diagnostic workup for pathogenic causes of premature adrenarche includes obtaining a bone age. Typically, if the bone age is <2SD above the child’s chronologic age, the signs of adrenarche are considered benign, and no fur ther workup is needed. However, a signifi cantly advanced bone age is commonly seen in individuals with premature adrenarche who have higher BMI and are taller [167]. Thus, using a criteria of a bone age > 2SD above the height age (the age corresponding to the child’s height when it is equal to the 50th per centile) may be a more useful criteria in chil dren with obesity and premature pubarche/ adrenarche.

### 33.2.5 Peripheral Metabolic

### Abnormalities in Obesity

Insulin has different weight-related effects depending on its location of action. Within the brain, insulin acts as a satiety signal,


## PDF page 903 | printed page 905

decreasing food intake through action in the hypothalamus [168]. However, insulin is also an extremely important inhibitor of lipolysis, thus promoting adipose tissue accumulation both directly at the level of the adipocyte and within the brain [169, 170]. In obesity, there is often, but not always, an increase in insulin levels. However, the increase in inflammation that also accompanies excess adipose tissue results in insulin resistance. Thus, satiating effects of increased insulin are not observed in obesity.

As mentioned above, leptin, discovered in 1994 and a product of the LEP gene (initially termed the ob gene in mice), is secreted by adi pocytes, and provides a signal to the central nervous system that adipose tissue is present. Leptin levels are correlated with the degree of obesity. Leptin receptors are present in the central nervous system in the hypothalamic regions known to regular hunger and satiety but are also present on various organs. Leptin deficiency results in severe, early onset obesity due to a lack of satiety [171]. Therefore, ele vated leptin levels in obesity should provide a protective mechanism against excessive adi pose accumulation by reducing appetite and reducing adiposity. However, this does not occur in those with obesity. Thus, there is some degree of leptin resistance that develops in obesity allowing for increased hunger in the setting of increased leptin. Interestingly, leptin is likely a major reason for elevated blood pressure in obesity [172].

Adiponectin is an adipocytokine that has protective metabolic effects. Elevated levels of adiponectin decrease the risk of myocardial infarction in adult men [173]. Unfortunately, instead of increasing as adipose tissue expands, adiponectin levels become lower as obesity increases in children and adolescents [174]. Low levels of adiponectin are predictive of adult type 2 diabetes [175], hypertension [176] and are associated in children with higher C-reactive protein and components of the metabolic syndrome [177].

Ghrelin, a known orexigenic hormone, is decreased in children with obesity and increases with weight loss [50, 53]. Thus, while ghrelin is likely not a causative agent in the

development of obesity, it likely plays a role in the failure of individuals to maintain weight loss.

### 33.2.6 Growth Hormone

### Abnormalities in Obesity

Obesity in childhood prior to puberty is asso ciated with taller stature than normal-weight peers [178, 179]. This seemingly obesityinduced height gain is attenuated in puberty, thus childhood obesity is not associated with taller stature in adulthood [178, 179]. Therefore, there appears to be an effect of excess adipose tissue on growth moderated by other hormonal milieu.

Interestingly, most studies, including a recent metaanalysis, have concluded that obe sity results in reduced basal and stimulated growth hormone levels [180–182]. Growth hormone levels in the range used to diagnose growth hormone deficiency are present in adults with obesity and are associated with increased dysmetabolic profiles and metaboli cally unfavorable adipose tissue distribution, including increased visceral adiposity [183, 184]. In fact, some studies have suggested that visceral adiposity (more than overall weight or body mass index) is associated with lower growth hormone levels [185, 186]. This asso ciation of low growth hormone levels with obesity is not surprising given that conditions causing primary growth hormone deficiency typically have increased adiposity, particu larly visceral adiposity, as a prominent fea ture. Reduced growth hormone secretion can be reversed with weight loss [187], supporting likely interactions between adipokines and the pituitary.

Obesity induces a reduction in growth hor mone secretion from the pituitary gland, but studies are mixed as to whether this results in a decrease, increase, or no change in total IGF-1 and/or free IGF-1 levels. This is an important practical point, as IGF-1 is often used to screen for growth hormone status, and growth hormone stimulation tests used to diagnose growth hormone deficiency in chil dren categorize significantly more children at

a higher (versus lower) BMI with growth hor mone deficiency [188]. This may also be influ enced by age as a recent study has shown younger children with obesity have higher IGF-1 levels, but during puberty these levels are decreased compared to peers [178].

The mechanisms that induce a reduction in growth hormone secretion in obesity are likely multifactorial and interrelated. The reduction in growth hormone may occur due to hyperinsulinemia, resulting in negative feedback on growth hormone production [189]. Other theories suggest that it is related to the hyperinsulinemia suppressing insulin-like growth factor-binding protein-1 (IGFBP-1), which, in term, modifies the free IGF-1 available and thus suppresses growth hormone secretion. However, studies are inconclusive when free IGF-1 is measured in the setting of obesity or acute overfeeding [190–192]. Some studies have suggested that free fatty acids are a primary factor in reduc tion of growth hormone levels in obesity. Free fatty acids are known to suppress growth hor mone production and are increased in obesity [193]. In an experimental design, the use of a medication known to reduce free fatty acids resulted in improved growth hormone secre tion in adults with obesity [194]. Free fatty acids may have a direct effect or act through somatostatin to decrease growth hormone in obesity [195]. Changes in ghrelin, a gutderived peptide that stimulates hunger and binds to the growth hormone secretagogue receptor and is lower in children with obesity compared to their normal-weight peers, may also play a role in the impact of obesity on growth hormone [196].

### 33

As noted above in the discussion of the adrenal axis, 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydro genase is present in adipose tissue and con verts cortisone to cortisol. Growth hormone plays a role in inhibiting this activity. Therefore, the reduction in growth hormone may also contribute to the increase in cortisol which then increases adiposity [197]. Therefore, the obesity induced reduction in growth hormone levels, like the increase in

insulin levels, may induce a vicious cycle, pro moting additional weight gain and increased adiposity, particularly visceral adiposity. Thus, it remains unclear whether the reduc tion in growth hormone secretion is a physio logic metabolically favorable development, inducing a reduction in glycemia, or an unfa vorable development, increasing visceral adi posity through reduced lipolysis and increasing inflammatory mediators. Supplementation of growth hormone or its stimulatory factors in obesity remains an area of active investigation.

### 33.2.7 Thyroid Hormone

### Abnormalities in Obesity

A mildly elevated TSH is often present in obe sity, causing clinical confusion as to whether this mild degree of compensated hypothyroid ism is a causative factor in the development of obesity or whether it is a result of weight gain. In general, only profound hypothyroidism causes rapid weight gain, and therefore, the mild TSH elevation in obesity is likely a con sequence of weight gain. A clinical clue is that hypothyroidism causes a reduction in linear growth, while obesity often promotes increased linear growth. Adipocytes have deiodinase activity and therefore participate in thyroid hormone metabolism, which may be a factor in these apparent abnormalities. In a study of children with obesity and normalweight children, the known mild elevation in TSH was demonstrated and noted to correlate with BMI, waist circumference, and lipid abnormalities [198]. Although the role of TSH elevations in weight gain is not clear, there are also associations of subclinical hypothyroidism with insulin resistance and multiple cardiometabolic risk factors [199]. Further studies are needed to determine whether mild alterations in thyroid function are causative factors in the metabolic changes seen with obesity. At this time there is no rec ommendation to treat these mild TSH eleva tions in children [200].

### 33.2.8 Hypothalamic-Pituitary-

### Ovarian/Testicular Axis in Obesity

Precocious puberty is more prevalent in girls with obesity compared to those of normal weight. This point had been controversial in earlier studies due to the criteria used to eval uate thelarche and concerns that adipose tis sue deposition may have been mistaken for evidence of early puberty. However, welldesigned studies [201–203] have documented earlier onset of both thelarche and menarche in girls with obesity. A more recent study has shown that the increased risk of central preco cious puberty in children with obesity is significant only when obesity has been present for over 2 years [204].

The impact of obesity on pubertal devel opment in boys has been less well-studied. However, a large investigation of over 4000 boys demonstrated a correlation between age of pubertal onset by testicular size and BMI. Boys with overweight and obesity were found to begin puberty and progress through puberty at an earlier age [205]. Despite some evidence supporting earlier pubertal progres sion in boys, obesity has also been associated with reductions in testosterone level and increased risk of gynecomastia, both lipomas tia and true breast development. This is thought to be due to the aromatization of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue. Thus, some degree of hypogonadism may be present in some adolescent males with obesity.

Mechanisms underlying earlier pubertal onset in children with obesity remain an area of active investigation. Leptin is known to be permissive in pubertal initiation and leptin deficiency results in a lack of pubertal changes. Leptin is also elevated in obesity. However, while leptin is permissive for puberty, it is not a causative factor. Additional mechanistic possibilities include hyperinsulinism leading to a suppression in sex hormone-binding globulin and thus increased bioavailability of sex steroids. The impact of androgens being aromatized to estrogens by adipose tissue has

also been postulated to play an important role in early pubertal changes in girls and may have variable impact on pubertal changes in boys.

Early hyperandrogenism and premature adrenarche are also more common in girls with obesity and have been linked in some populations to an increased risk of progres sion to PCOS in adolescence and adulthood [206].

Obesity also impacts conception and preg nancy/birth complications. High BMI is asso ciated with reduced semen quality [207]. PCOS can impact female fertility and is asso ciated with obesity and insulin resistance (dis cussed in depth in Chap. 28). Obesity during pregnancy increases risks of pre eclampsia, miscarriage, and congenital abnor malities [208].

### 33.2.9 Other Pituitary Hormone

### Abnormalities in Obesity

Prolactin, a hormone crucial for lactation, may also regulate energy metabolism [209]. Prolactin levels are increased in adults with overweight or obesity and higher levels are associated with metabolically beneficial pro files [210]. This may be in part due to eleva tions of prolactin being associated with visceral fat mass, a more metabolically detri mental fat depot [211].

Oxytocin, another hormone important for lactation but also for normal birth processes, is synthesized in both the brain and the gas trointestinal tract and has important meta bolic actions [212]. Genetic polymorphisms in the oxytocin gene have been linked to obesity in adolescents [213]. Additionally, low oxyto cin levels in adolescents are correlated with higher hyperphagia scores [213], indicating a possible association between satiety and oxy tocin. This association is supported by animal studies which show oxytocin signals through receptors in the brain to activate the POMC pathway and induce satiation [214]; however, it is notable that animal models lacking oxyto

On the other hand, oxytocin can impact muscle development [216], inhibit the development of adipocytes [217], stimulate lipolysis [218], and promote increased energy expenditure [219]. Small clinical trials have shown that intranasal oxytocin may signifi cantly reduce hunger and/or food intake [220] and possibly reduce BMI [221], which has led to additional clinical trials underway to deter mine the therapeutic usefulness of oxytocin in obese states.

### 33.2.10 Skeletal Impact of Obesity

As described in detail above, AN, a condition of extreme underweight and nutritional defi ciency, results in a reduction in bone mineral density. However, the opposite extreme, ele vated weight in obesity also leads to changes in bone density and structure [222]. Most studies, including metaanalyses, show increased bone mineral density in individuals with obesity [223–225]. Despite the reassur ing trends in bone density, children with obe sity may be at increased risk for reduced bone strength [226] and fractures [227, 228]. Increased adiposity may cause alterations at the level of the bone through inflammatory markers and mediators. Furthermore, as adi pocytes and osteoblasts are both derived from a common progenitor mesenchymal stem cell, an alteration in one cell type may contribute to alterations in the other [229]. It is well-documented that 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are lower in individuals with obesity, attributable to both reduced dietary intake and increased distribution in adipose tissue. However, whether or not lower vitamin D levels in children with obesity are associated with fracture risk remains controversial [230, 231].

### 33

Visceral adiposity, the more metabolically active and detrimental fat depot compared to subcutaneous adiposity, appears to be detri mental to bone health. Higher levels of vis ceral fat have been found to correlate with lower bone density in both adolescent girls [232] and women [233] with obesity.

### 33.2.11 Patient Evaluation

The evaluation of a child with obesity starts with an analysis of the weight/BMI trajectory over the patient’s life. Physicians should iden tify whether obesity was severe prior to age 5 years, a marker of possible genetic forms of obesity, or whether there were any inflection points marking a significant change that exac erbated weight gain. In general, the medical history evaluation focuses on determining whether or not there are red flags for genetic forms of obesity or undiagnosed comorbidi ties that need to be addressed. Further, the family history should elucidate any strong family history of severe obesity, bariatric sur gery, or other familial disorders (i.e., vision problems, developmental delays, or pregnancy losses). Additionally, a history of consanguin ity in the family increases the risk for genetic disorders. Current medical problems and past medical history may reveal other hints for syndromic features associated with obesity, such as developmental or cognitive delays, learning disabilities, vision difficulties, or organ abnormalities. The review of systems screens for comorbidities such as headaches for pseudotumor cerebri, joint pain for ortho paedic problems, fatigue for obstructive sleep apnea, or polyuria/polydipsia for diabetes. In the physical exam, care is taken to identify signs of comorbidities such as elevated blood pressure, acanthosis, abnormal optic discs, or hepatomegaly. There are several excellent guidelines which give additional detail for the work-up of childhood obesity [234–237].

Guidelines differ regarding laboratory rec ommendations for childhood obesity. In gen eral, guidelines point to starting screening for obesity comorbidities at age six with an ALT, lipid panel, and haemoglobin A1c, although the recent American Academy of Pediatrics obesity guidelines recommend screening only in those 10 years and older for ALT and abnormal glucose metabolism [238]. However, there is evidence that individuals less than age 6 years can have evidence of obesity-related diseases [239]. Thus, physicians may want to consider testing earlier than the current rec ommendations depending on the specific sce

### 33.2.12 Management

First-line treatment for obesity and related metabolic factors is behavioral change sup ported by family-centered, multidisciplinary treatment in individual and/or group settings. The goal of behavioral change is to imple ment an improved diet, targeting reducing the glycemic index in foods, increasing intake of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins and healthy fats while eliminating sugar containing bever ages and significantly reducing intake of pro cessed carbohydrates. Physical activity with a goal of 60 min daily, including 30 min three times per week of moderate to vigorous activ ity, can improve insulin resistance and the inflammatory profile even without inducing weight loss. The most recent US Preventative Task Force analysis on obesity in children and adolescents states that only comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions with at least 26 contact hours were successful for weight loss [236]. Thus, multi-component and multi-specialty/disciplinary programs are instrumental in the treatment of childhood obesity.

Second-line therapies can include medica tions and, in some cases, bariatric surgery. Pharmacotherapy in childhood obesity is underutilized [240], especially given the failure of lifestyle modifications to effectively cause changes at the population level. Expert opin

ion suggests pharmacotherapy initiation could be considered in individuals with obe sity who have not had success with lifestyle interventions and who agree to long-term therapy if efficacy outcomes are met (≥5% BMI reduction from baseline after 12 weeks on optimal dose) [241]. Unfortunately, there are only a small number of pharmacotherapy options available for those at least 12 years of age. The currently approved medications (as of 2023) include orlistat (a lipase inhibitor), liraglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist), sema glutide (a weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist), and phentermine/topiramate (a combination stimulant and anticonvulsant). Orlistat, along with behavioral modification, can induce 19% of subjects to have a 5% or greater weight loss, with 9.5% of subjects losing more than 10% of body weight in clinical trials [242]. Liraglutide resulted in 43% of adolescents attaining a ≥5% BMI change with 26% achiev ing at least 10% BMI loss [243]. At the highest dose, 46% of adolescents taking phentermine/ topiramate achieved at least 5% BMI reduc tion and 42% achieved 10% or more BMI loss [244]. Semaglutide resulted in a 5% or more BMI reduction in 76% of adolescents with obesity, with 63% of subjects experiencing a 10% or more BMI loss [245]. Bariatric surgery is also being performed in adolescents, and in recent published data, the results and side effects appear to be similar to those docu mented in adults when performed at experi enced centers [246]. At 5 years, patients had an average weight reduction of 26%, and over 75% had more than a 20% weight loss. The large majority of patients had resolution of diabetes (86%), hypertension (68%), and hypertriglyceridemia (81%). The most com mon complications were micronutrient defi ciencies with potential implications for bone health, and 20% of patients needed an addi tional abdominal surgical procedure.
